To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
expertise with homogeneous categories (birds and cars) recruits the fusiform face area more than expertise with familiar objects (e.g., tools and furniture).

(a) expertise with birds and cars recruits face-selective brain areas, the fusiform gyrity (FFA) in the temporal lobe and the occipital face area (OFA) in the occipital lobar; (b) expertise with birds activates the right FFA more than expertise with cars; (c) expertise with cars activates the right OFA more than expertise with birds; (d) the right FFA is activated more for birds than cars in both groups
the fusiform face area (FFA) is activated when people look at objects that they have become experts in, such as cars, and this is true even if these objects do not resemble faces.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of object perception.
the question how expertise for objects and categories influences brain activity and how brain activity can be used to measure expertise.
the neural basis of expertise and the mechanisms that underlie the development of expertise.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fusiform face area is not specialized for faces per se, but for the processing of any category of objects that is learned and processed at a fine-grained level.
the FFA is not a face area but a category-selective area that responds more strongly to familiar than novel objects.
expertise for unfamiliar objects (greebles) recruits the face-selective regions, while expertise for familiar objects (cars) recruits face-selective regions to a lesser extent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FFA is not only specialized to represent faces and objects, but also to represent expertise with these entities.
expertise for cars and birds recruit brain areas involved in recognizing faces.
expertise with homogeneous categories recruits brain areas involved with face recognition, and that the FFA is involved in expertise with homogeneous categories.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the right fusiform gyrus and OFA are not face-selective areas, but rather they are involved in processing objects in a category-selective manner.
the right FFA is involved in processing objects of expertise, and that this involvement is independent from the superficial properties of the objects.
the FFA is not specialized for faces per se, but for the recognition of any category with sufficient homogeneity.
